A dwarf planet is a planetary-mass object that is neither a planet nor a natural satellite. That is, it is in direct orbit of the Sun, and is massive enough for its shape to be in hydrostatic equilibrium under its own gravity, but has not cleared the neighborhood around its orbit.

Also, NASA did not reclassify, the IAU did and by the IAU I mean only 5% of them voted on the matter.

Space.com

The vote involved just 424 astronomers who remained for the last day of a meeting of the International Astronomical Union (IAU) in Prague.

"I'm embarassed for astornomy," said Alan Stern, leader of NASA's New Horizon's mission to Pluto and a scientist at the Southwest Research Institute. "Less than 5 percent of the world's astronomers voted."

Stern, in charge of the robotic probe on its way to Pluto, said the language of the resolution is flawed. It requires that a planet "has cleared the neighborhood around its orbit." But Earth, Mars, Jupiter and Neptune all have asteroids as neighbors.

"It's patently clear that Earth's zone is not cleared," Stern told SPACE.com. "Jupiter has 50,000 trojan asteroids," which orbit in lockstep with the planet.

Stern called it "absurd" that only 424 astronomers were allowed to vote, out of some 10,000 professional astronomers around the globe.

Currently, the version of ASP.NET MVC that Voat runs on only runs on Windows. The next version of ASP.NET MVC has full Linux support as promised by Microsoft no less. I maintain a couple of large distributed programming OSS projects in .NET and demand for Mono support has been rising steadily over the past couple of years because it's being used in production systems more regularly even for server-side stuff these days.

To my experience - aiming to create massive load website and base it on Windows servers seems a bit expensive?

.NET has a very different scaling model than OSS stacks like Python / Ruby / Node.JS. I've maintained large-scale systems (500 mbs of event data per second coming through our API) in .NET that are running on as few as 8-10 boxes (doesn't count the big Cassandra cluster those systems used, just the .NET front-end.)

If you really want to understand it, read HighScalability's excellent series on StackOverflow's architecture.

If you want a TL;DR; - most OSS stacks are complete and utter dogshit when it comes to parallelism and concurrency. Python and Ruby have no concept of threading, for instance. So they scale out by running multiple processes per machine (1 per core usually) and lots of cheap, commodity machines per application.

.NET, on the other hand, has the best built-in concurrency tools out of any general purpose programming runtime (source: I port concurrent programming frameworks from JVM to .NET / CLR for a living) - so it scales by maximizing the hardware that it's on using threads, kernel caching, and etc. .NET scales vertically - by running on better hardware, not more of it.

Windows/.NET so additional numbers on comparisons in terms of performance

I wish I could find the Curse.com migration from Python to .NET case study, because that had excellent numbers. Ran on something like 1/6th the machines at a much smaller level of utilization. .NET actually has amazing performance per hardware footprint, although on Linux Mono not nearly as good as the JVM in performance terms, although that's starting to change due to Microsoft OSS-ing their garbage collector and other stuff, which is making it's way into Mono starting with Mono 4.0.
